extracted.intended_audience: Writers new to using beta readers; writers of any book-length genre with a completed manuscript or currently drafting who want to use beta readers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for finding, commissioning, managing, and responding to beta readers for book-length manuscripts, including what to expect from beta feedback and how to use it in revision. The material covers both author and reader perspectives, logistics, etiquette, and tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: The differences between a beta reader, critique partner, and editor
rubrics_metrics.description: The differences between a beta reader, critique partner, and editor
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify how the type of feedback and role expectations differ across these three relationships so you can select appropriate readers and interpret notes correctly. The course promises to explain reasonable expectations for feedback from a beta and how that differs from critique partners or professional editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal beta reader qualifications
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance on what makes a 'right reader for your specific project' — e.g., demographic/genre familiarity, reading habits, prior experience — so feedback is relevant and actionable. The class will provide a list of places to look for readers and attributes to seek.

rubrics_metrics.name: When it’s time to find beta readers
rubrics_metrics.description: When it’s time to find readers
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice on timing in the revision process (when a manuscript is ready for reader feedback vs. still in drafting), including an observation that the first step can be simple but is a major milestone. Includes guidance on when to solicit feedback versus continuing to revise alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where to find beta readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Where to connect with potential readers online or face-to-face
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical places and channels (online communities, face-to-face groups, paid platforms) to recruit beta readers. The course supplies a post-class list of places to look for beta readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to ask someone to beta read
rubrics_metrics.description: The (not as scary as you think) way to ask someone to beta read
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scripts and sample language to request beta reading, including suggested wording, how to set expectations in the initial ask, and sample templates provided after class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time guidelines and realistic turnaround requests
rubrics_metrics.description: Time guidelines (saving yourself time and realistic turnaround requests)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: How to estimate reasonable turnaround times for readers, how to structure deadlines, and how to avoid unrealistic time expectations. Includes strategies to expedite the beta reader process and save author time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using electronic vs. paper-based feedback
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparative pros/cons and best practices for collecting feedback digitally or on paper (e.g., comment tools, annotation workflows). The course discusses formats and how they affect the feedback process.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to provide clear instructions for your beta reader
rubrics_metrics.description: How to provide clear instructions for your beta reader
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exact instructions and templates to give readers (what to look for, the level of detail desired, scene-level versus overall notes). After-class handouts include clear instructions to share with your beta readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: What to expect from a beta reader (sample feedback)
rubrics_metrics.description: What to expect from a beta reader (sample feedback)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of sample feedback so authors know the form and substance of helpful notes. The class provides sample feedback files to demonstrate typical beta-reader responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: What to do with beta reader feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: What to do with beta reader feedback
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Workflow and decision-making guidance for interpreting, prioritizing, and implementing feedback — including how to differentiate between actionable patterns and subjective preference, and when to ignore suggestions.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to continue an ongoing beta reader relationship
rubrics_metrics.description: How to continue an ongoing beta reader relationship
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best practices for maintaining long-term beta-reader collaborations: communication frequency, reciprocity, follow-up, expressing appreciation, and evolving expectations over multiple projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making graceful exits / when to 'break up' with a reader
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance and sample scripts for the rare occasions when you may want to end a relationship with a beta reader, including how to 'break up' professionally and preserve reputation. Post-class materials include scripts for breaking up with beta readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major beta-reading platforms
rubrics_metrics.description: Some of the major beta reading platforms
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overview of prominent platforms and marketplaces where authors can find beta readers, including considerations for selection, cost, and reliability. The course lists platforms and discusses pros/cons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Considerations for paying beta readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Considerations if you should/want to pay for beta readers
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pros and cons of paid beta feedback (cost vs. quality/responsibility), what paying buys you (e.g., guaranteed turnaround), and guidance on setting scope and expectations for paid readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to respond when asked to be a beta reader
rubrics_metrics.description: How to respond when you are asked to be a beta reader
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the reader’s perspective: how to accept or opt out, how to set limits and turnaround expectations, and what kinds of notes are helpful to the author. The class covers reader etiquette and responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to opt out of a project and types of helpful notes
rubrics_metrics.description: How to opt out of a project you don’t want to read; the types of notes that are helpful to the author
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance for beta readers on declining requests politely and on delivering constructive, actionable notes (examples of useful note types). Emphasizes clarity and respect for author/editorial needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coaching readers through the best way to help you (step-by-step from initial ask to feedback)
rubrics_metrics.description: As the author it’s important for you to coach your readers through the best way for them to help you; step-by-step guidance from the initial ask to the feedback process
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A structured, author-led process to onboard beta readers: initial ask, instructions, deadlines, examples of desired feedback, and follow-up. The class promises step-by-step coaching materials and templates.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to talk about feedback and when to step away
rubrics_metrics.description: When it’s time to talk about feedback, and when it’s time to step away
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance on timing conversations about feedback (when to solicit, when to debrief) and on recognizing when to pause or step away from feedback cycles to avoid over-revision or fatigue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goals of beta-reader feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: This stage of revision allows you to learn where your story can improve, what you are doing well, and if your manuscript is coming across the way you intended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines the core purposes of beta feedback: identify problem areas, confirm strengths, and test whether the manuscript communicates the intended story/impact. Use this as the evaluative lens when reading beta notes.
